analysis.one_liner: Raises Social Security benefits and funds them with payroll taxes on income above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee from January 30, 2019 until the Congress ended on January 3, 2021, with just one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would increase Social Security benefits across the board, switch cost-of-living adjustments to a price index built for seniors' spending, and raise the minimum benefit for long-time low earners to the poverty line. To pay for it, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages and self-employment income above $400,000 — which are currently exempt — and slowly raise the payroll tax rate on all workers and employers. It also raises the income level at which Social Security benefits become taxable.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries. Every beneficiary would get an immediate benefit increase. Seniors would get cost-of-living adjustments keyed to what seniors actually buy, which historically runs higher than the index used today. Retirees with 30 or more years of work at low wages would be guaranteed a benefit near the poverty line, and long-career low earners get a sliding-scale minimum. Middle-income seniors would pay tax on fewer of their benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries, especially low earners

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises every beneficiary's benefit by changing the benefit formula factor from 90% to 93% of average indexed earnings, effective for months after December 2019.

Cost-of-living adjustments would be calculated using a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers that the Bureau of Labor Statistics would publish, replacing the index tied to younger workers' spending.
Workers with 11 to 30 or more years of work would get a minimum benefit scaled up to a share of the poverty line, reaching 125% of the poverty guideline at 30 or more years of work.
Earnings and self-employment income above $400,000 would become subject to Social Security taxes, and the bill counts those earnings slightly in the benefit formula for new beneficiaries.
The payroll tax rate paid by employees, employers, and the self-employed would rise gradually from 6.2%/12.4% to 7.4%/14.8% between 2020 and after 2042.
The income level at which Social Security benefits become taxable would rise to $50,000 for single filers and $100,000 for joint filers.
Increased benefits would not count as income for Medicaid, CHIP, or SSI eligibility, so beneficiaries would not lose other aid because their Social Security check went up.

analysis.who_pays: The highest earners: income above $400,000 would face Social Security payroll taxes that today stop at roughly $132,900. All workers and employers would also pay a gradually rising rate over two decades. Employers' matching share could come partly out of wages or hiring.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, plus all workers and employers slowly

drawbacks.text: The bill raises payroll taxes on every worker and every employer, not just the wealthy: the employee and employer rates each climb from 6.2% to 7.4% over roughly 24 years.
The employer share of the higher tax is a cost of employment, and businesses can pass part of such payroll costs to workers through slower wage growth or to consumers through prices.

Beneficiaries with earnings above $400,000 would see only a small return (2% of excess earnings) in the benefit formula for the added taxes they pay, meaning the change is mostly a tax increase at the top.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are concrete and broad: larger checks, a more accurate inflation adjustment for seniors, and a poverty-level floor for career low earners, plus a merged, fully funded trust fund. The costs are also real: a slowly rising payroll tax on every working American and their employer, and a steep new tax on income above $400,000. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much weight you put on protecting the trust fund's solvency against raising payroll taxes, but the benefit increases and the funding are explicitly linked in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2019, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Blumenthal introduced the Social Security 2100 Act in the Senate on January 30, 2019, joined by one cosponsor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the action history through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners with income above $400,000 keep that income free of Social Security tax, and employers avoid the gradually rising payroll rate. Social Security beneficiaries get none of the proposed increases, and the trust fund's long-term funding gap is left unaddressed.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senator from Connecticut; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security 2100 Act in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsor it drew in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred on January 30, 2019; it died there.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists; both Senate supporters were Democrats and the committee that buried it was run by a Republican majority.

industries.industry: High earners and high-income self-employed (income above $400,000)
industries.note: The bill subjects their income above $400,000 to Social Security payroll taxes for the first time, which is the main funding source for the benefit increases ordinary beneficiaries would receive.
Employers would pay a matching payroll tax that rises from 6.2% to 7.4% on wages over about two decades, though the burden applies only to wages below the existing cap plus earnings above $400,000.
Every covered worker would pay a slowly rising tax (6.2% to 7.4% by 2043) in exchange for a stronger, fully funded Social Security system and, eventually, higher benefits of their own.
